chapters.1: The Preacher (traditionally Solomon) opens by declaring that everything in life is fleeting and repetitive, like the sun rising and setting, rivers flowing to the sea, and generations coming and going. He says he pursued wisdom deeply but found that greater knowledge only brought greater sorrow, concluding that life under the sun feels endlessly circular and ultimately unsatisfying.
chapters.2: The Preacher describes testing pleasure, massive building projects, wealth, and entertainment to see if any of it brings lasting satisfaction, and concludes it's all 'vanity' because death erases the distinction between the wise and the foolish. He decides the simple, attainable good in life is to enjoy food, drink, and the fruit of one's work as gifts from God.
chapters.3: This chapter contains the famous poem on timing: a season for everything, including birth and death, planting and uprooting, war and peace. The Preacher reflects that God has set eternity in people's hearts yet made his larger plan unknowable, and concludes that enjoying one's work and the present moment is the best a person can do.
chapters.4: The Preacher observes the oppression of the powerless and decides the dead may be better off than the living who must endure it, then notes the loneliness of working only for oneself with no one to share the reward. He praises companionship ('two are better than one') and ends by noting that even popularity and power eventually fade and are forgotten.
chapters.5: This chapter gives practical advice about approaching God: don't make rash vows or babble in prayer, and if you make a vow, keep it. It also warns that loving money never satisfies and that wealth can bring restless anxiety, concluding again that enjoying the modest portion God gives is the realistic path to contentment.
chapters.6: The Preacher describes the tragedy of a person who has wealth and honor but no ability to actually enjoy it, saying even an unborn child who sees nothing of life might be better off. He repeats that human appetite and desire are never fully satisfied, and that no one truly knows what is good for a person during their brief, shadow-like life.
chapters.7: This chapter offers a collection of sobering wisdom sayings, such as valuing a good reputation over luxury, learning more from sorrow and rebuke than from laughter and flattery, and avoiding both excessive self-righteousness and excessive wickedness. The Preacher admits that true wisdom and a truly upright person are hard to find, since everyone has some flaw.
chapters.8: The Preacher advises respecting those in authority and not rashly opposing a king, while acknowledging that justice in the world is uneven and often delayed, letting wicked people seem to get away with wrongdoing for a time. He concludes that, ultimately, those who fear God will fare better, even though the full workings of God's plan remain beyond human understanding.
chapters.9: The Preacher notes that the same fate, death, comes to everyone regardless of how righteous or wicked, wise or foolish they are, so he urges people to enjoy their food, relationships, and work energetically while they're alive. He adds that success in life often comes down to timing and chance rather than skill alone, illustrated by a poor wise man who saves a city but is quickly forgotten.
chapters.10: This chapter is a string of proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly, including warnings about a little folly undoing a reputation, fools exposing themselves through speech, and what happens when rulers are foolish or incompetent (like a land cursed with a childish king). It closes with a caution against laziness and against cursing a king or the rich even in private thought, since word travels.
chapters.11: The Preacher encourages generous, forward-looking action, 'casting bread on the waters,' and diversifying effort since no one can know in advance what will succeed. He urges young people to enjoy their youth and its vitality, while still remembering they are accountable to God for how they live.
chapters.12: The book closes with a vivid, poetic picture of the body aging and failing, bones trembling, eyes dimming, as a reminder to honor God while young and before old age and death arrive. The Preacher repeats that everything is fleeting, and gives his final conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments, because God will ultimately judge every deed, even the hidden ones.
